title: Start-up costs, cash runway and business banking
audience: Owners planning the money side of a new Australian property trade business, before the first invoice
learningOutcomes: List the one-off and recurring costs of starting a trade business, and separate the essential costs from the later ones.
Estimate how many months of living and business costs the owner can cover before income is steady.
Set up separate business banking and a receipt routine that supports the tax records.

instruction.heading: Sorting the costs into types
instruction.body: Start with five groups: registration and licensing fees set by the state or territory, insurance premiums, website and online listing costs, marketing materials, and equipment. Add a sixth group for transport, phone and data, and software for accounts or bookings. Inside each group, separate one-off costs, such as a first set of tools or a logo, from recurring costs, such as insurance premiums, subscriptions or a phone plan. Enter each amount only after you have checked it with the supplier or the authority, and record the date of the check. Leave out any amount you cannot yet check. Do not copy a figure from a guide. The guide this lesson draws on gives US-based amounts, and those are not used here.

instruction.heading: Deciding what is needed now
instruction.body: Mark each cost as needed before the first job, needed within the first three months, or needed later. Few trade businesses need every item on the first day. A vehicle the owner already has, a basic phone plan and a simple booking method may cover the first jobs, provided the required registration and insurance are in place. Items that protect against serious loss, such as insurance and any required registration, come first. Items that add convenience, such as a larger tool set or a paid advertising campaign, can wait until work is coming in.

instruction.heading: Working out the cash runway
instruction.body: Cash runway is the number of months the owner can keep paying living costs and business costs before the business earns enough to cover them. Add the monthly living costs, the monthly business costs and an allowance for the months with little work. Divide the cash set aside by that monthly total. Set the allowance honestly. The first months of a trade business are often slower than the owner expects, and a plan that assumes full work from the first week is fragile. If the runway is short, delay the start, reduce the start-up list, or keep some paid work while the business builds.

instruction.heading: Keeping business money and records separate
instruction.body: Open a separate business bank account before the first invoice, and pay business costs and receive business income through it. Keep every receipt, and write down the business purpose of each purchase. Mixing personal and business money makes records hard to check and creates problems at tax time. Avoid funding the start with expensive debt where a cheaper option exists. Speak with a registered tax agent about which costs are deductible and how vehicle expenses are recorded.

procedure: List the one-off and recurring costs in the six groups, and mark each as checked (with a source and date) or leave it out until it is checked.
Mark each cost as needed before the first job, needed within three months, or needed later.
Add the monthly living costs, the monthly business costs and an allowance for slow months.
Divide the cash set aside by the monthly total to find the runway in months.
Open a separate business account, and set up a receipt routine that records the date and business purpose of each purchase.
Book a review with a registered tax agent to confirm the deductions and record-keeping rules.

workedExamples.situation: An owner has set aside six months of living costs. The owner plans a vehicle purchase in month one, while an insurance premium and a website cost are due before the first job.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the vehicle purchase go ahead in month one?
workedExamples.reasoning: The insurance premium and any required registration come first, because they protect the owner and the client before work starts. The vehicle purchase should be tested against the runway. If it uses a large share of the cash set aside, the owner may run short before income is steady. Using the existing vehicle for early jobs and reviewing the purchase after three months is the safer option.

equipmentAndPpe: Cost register, on paper or in a spreadsheet, with the date and source of each amount
Receipt folder or a scanning app, with a dated filing routine

commonErrors.error: Leaving out recurring costs such as insurance, software and phone plans.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep a monthly section in the cost register, and review it every quarter.

commonErrors.error: Calculating the runway with no allowance for slow months.
commonErrors.prevention: Add a slow-month allowance and test the runway against it.

commonErrors.error: Paying business and personal costs from one account.
commonErrors.prevention: Open the business account before the first invoice, and pay all business costs from it.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The GST registration threshold is $75,000 of GST turnover, as the ATO states on its page checked on 2026-11-02. Check them with the ATO or a registered tax agent.
State and territory registration and licence fees differ between jurisdictions.

qualityStandard: Every cost is marked as checked, with a source and date, or is left out.
The runway is calculated from monthly totals and includes a slow-month allowance.
A separate business account and a receipt routine are set up before the first invoice.
documentationEvidence: Cost register with one-off and recurring items, sources and check dates
Runway calculation with monthly totals and the slow-month allowance
Record of the business account opening and the receipt routine
summary: Separate one-off costs from recurring costs, and mark what is needed first.
Plan the cash runway with a slow-month allowance rather than a best case.
Keep business money separate, and record the purpose of every purchase.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which costs should be funded first when cash is limited?
options: Marketing campaigns and a logo and a website with a photo gallery and a video reel
A premium tool set for future projects and a van with a full branded wrap and lettering
Insurance and any required registration, because they protect the owner and clients before work starts
A vehicle upgrade, because it looks professional and a bigger trailer for the whole crew to use

knowledgeChecks.question: How is cash runway calculated?
options: Total cash divided by the monthly total of living and business costs, with a slow-month allowance included
Total income divided by a count of completed jobs for the year and the tools bought in it
Monthly business costs multiplied by the number of tools and the cost of every van ever bought
Cash set aside minus the price of the first quote and the cost of the first van lease paid

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should business and personal money stay in separate accounts?
options: It lets the owner avoid registering the business
It removes the need to keep receipts
It keeps business records clear and easier to check
It guarantees the business will make a profit
